bull_bear.body: The INR 1,500 cr QIP is the defining capital event: **75% to debt reduction**, balance to general corporate purposes, taking the company to net cash INR 483 cr. Institutional holding reached a historic-high 33%. Beyond deleveraging, capital goes to a modest INR 500 cr/yr equipment programme and the $100 mn US connectivity facility over five years — i.e. capital-light growth funded by utilisation and de-bottlenecking rather than greenfield. Working capital is a stated focus, "engaging into dialogues with the customers on reducing the payment terms." Notably absent: any large capacity capex despite an order book that is 2.4x larger and a demand environment where lead times are tightening.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Raw-material availability is the binding operational risk.** Germanium sourcing is "work in progress over the next few quarters"; helium is being watched against Middle East developments. Management is taking orders "keeping in mind the availability of our raw materials" — i.e. the order book is already being rationed against input risk.
- **Capacity is the second constraint** — orders are being picked and chosen; ex-anchor intake fell from INR 7,000-8,000 cr to ~INR 3,000 cr. If de-bottlenecking underdelivers, the order book converts more slowly.
- **Order-book concentration:** the $1.1 bn hyperscaler deal is a very large share of the INR 18,618 cr book, and INR 16,390 cr of it executes in Q3 FY27 *and beyond* — the near-term executable slice is only INR 2,228 cr.
- **Hyperscaler capex cyclicality**, plus the analyst-raised question of Chinese token-cost deflation compressing the AI capex environment. Management's answer was macro-thesis-based (cloud revenues accelerating, demand outstripping supply) but conceded "the price points will have to become more efficient" and "there has to be something that has to give at some level."
- **No revenue guidance at all** — management repeated they don't guide and cannot say how much they will grow from here.
- Europe DC investment "progress and speed on the ground is still slow"; framed as "a dark horse" that scales in a year or two — i.e. 25% of revenue sits in a region management describes as behind.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident and specific where it counts — raised two guidance items (margin 20%→23%, DC+Enterprise mix 30%→50%) rather than merely reaffirming, and pre-emptively corrected an analyst who was reading the executable order book as revenue guidance. Disclosure discipline is consistent and pre-declared: capacity utilisation, realisation, germanium contracting terms and segment margin splits are all refused "for competitive reasons," which is defensible but does limit verification. The most credible moment was the CFO answering the gross-margin question honestly against interest — acknowledging raw-material pressure rather than attributing flat gross margin to mix timing. Ankit Agarwal's answer on the AI/telecom balance was strategically thoughtful rather than promotional, explicitly wanting the telecom and rural (BharatNet/BEAD) books as ballast against DC cyclicality.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **Ex the anchor deal, order intake actually decelerated** — INR ~3,000 cr this quarter vs INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter. The CFO's framing (capacity-driven selectivity, not demand weakness) is plausible given the "pick and choose" comment, but it is the number to watch if utilisation improves and intake does *not* recover.
- **Margin was raised while gross margin was flat.** The entire 20%→23% bridge sits below the gross line: utilisation, mix, attach rate. That makes the attach-rate milestones (>20% in Q2, 25% by Q4) the most load-bearing checkable commitments on the call.
- **STL is deliberately capital-light into a demand boom** — INR 500 cr/yr of upgrades against an INR 18,618 cr book. It is choosing de-bottlenecking over greenfield, which protects returns but caps how much of the AI cycle it can capture.
- The **$100 mn US facility is a connectivity plant, not fibre capacity** — it does not add cable/fibre tonnage; its purpose is onshore turnaround speed and product customisation for US DC customers.
- Management explicitly closed the door on transceivers and semiconductors, the two adjacencies the market most often extrapolates for an AI-DC optical play.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Integrates glass science with precision manufacturing to co-create advanced high-density, low-latency optical solutions
- Claims first-mover next-generation fibre products - India's first Hollow Core Fibre cable and a 4-core Multi-Core Fibre Unitube cable launched in the UK

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Supply chain and manufacturing concentration risk — Given the global scope of operations, disruptions in manufacturing, delivery or logistics can adversely affect revenue and reputation; the company also relies on a single or limited source for certain input materials, with global shifts affecting availability of rare earth materials
- Geopolitical and trade/regulatory risk — Exposure to macroeconomic and geopolitical risks including wars/conflicts, political uncertainty, and regulatory changes such as reciprocal tariffs and anti-dumping duties that can affect demand and competitiveness; commodity price volatility can also influence operational and financial performance
- Industry/strategic execution risk - customer capex dependence — STL's business depends on capital expenditure by telecom operators and investments in data centres by enterprises and hyperscalers; the company may not be able to implement its strategy successfully and deliver growth if industry dynamics change
- Product portfolio and innovation risk — Risk that STL may be unable to develop new products/solutions that proactively meet customers' unmet needs; competitors launching new or technologically improved products could put the company's prospects at risk
- Customer and competition risk — The market is competitive with few barriers to capacity expansion by existing and new players; most contracts are awarded via competitive bidding, making pricing an important factor
- Talent management risk — Successful strategy execution is highly dependent on the company's ability to attract, develop, engage and retain top professional talent
- Cyber security risk — Increasing sophistication of cyber threats exposes the company to data theft, ransomware, business interruption from malware/phishing, and data privacy breaches
- Financial risks (currency, interest rate, liquidity, counterparty) — Exposure to foreign currency fluctuations, interest rate movements on Indian and foreign-currency borrowings, liquidity needs for operations and growth investments, and counterparty/credit risk on receivables and investments
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Data Center: 21% of Q1 revenue, up from 1% in FY26** — the single largest mix shift in the business.
- **Telecom & Citizen Networks** remains the core pillar; management is deliberate about keeping it as the counterweight to DC cyclicality.
- **Geography:** North America expanded to 54% of revenue (from 39% in FY26), Europe 25%, RoW 22%. CRU's North America CAGR forecast to 2030 was upgraded from 15% to **18.6%**.
- **US onshore:** South Carolina facility supports the Neuralis MMC pre-terminated launch; the new $100 mn investment is a connectivity (not fibre-capacity) facility — "it doesn't really translate into a capacity per se."
- Businesses deliberately exited: active components, multiple other lines, and the system-integration business (demerged) — "a very conscious choice to be very, very focused on the optical fiber cable connectivity side."

latest_quarter.body: EBITDA margin of ~20.8% was achieved a full year ahead of the previous guide, but **gross margin was broadly flat sequentially despite a richer DC mix** — the CFO attributed this squarely to input costs: "the prices of the key raw material getting increased to significant multiples" in the war situation. The three named raw-material exposures are **germanium** (glass process — dual response of diversifying sources *and* developing technology to reduce consumption per unit), **helium** (fibre manufacturing — recycling technology already in place, watching Middle East developments closely), and **polyethylene** (oil-linked, and "up to a certain level… we are able to pass that on to our customers"). The path to 23% is therefore three levers management named explicitly: higher factory utilisation, better product/customer mix, and the attach-rate climb from 16% → 20%+ → 25%. DC solutions carry structurally higher margins than telecom, which management confirmed without quantifying.
latest_quarter.title: Margins & cost dynamics

latest_quarter.body:
- **Q4 FY26 (prior):** order book INR 7.3k cr; **targeting 20% EBITDA margin by end of FY27**; FY26 inflows doubled to INR 7,687 cr; ~INR 500 cr capex planned for technology upgrades and high-value DC portfolio; DC + Enterprise guided at 30% of revenue.
- **Q1 FY27 (this):** *Guidance beaten and raised:* the 20% EBITDA margin target for end-FY27 was **hit in Q1** and the target **raised to 23%**; DC+Enterprise mix guidance **raised from 30% to 50%** of FY27 revenue. *Delivered:* INR 500 cr/yr capex confirmed and extended to a 3-year INR 1,500 cr programme; DC revenue share went 1% (FY26) → 21%. *Step-change:* Q1 order intake of INR 13,100 cr = 1.7x all of FY26; open order book INR 18,618 cr (+2.4x QoQ) vs INR 7.3k cr last quarter; net-debt-free after a INR 1,500 cr QIP (75% to debt reduction); ICRA upgrade to AA Stable. *New commitments:* attach rate >20% from Q2 FY27 and 25% by Q4 FY27; $100 mn US connectivity plant over 5 years (phasing TBD); $1.1 bn hyperscaler contract running to FY29. *Watch:* gross margin flat despite mix, on germanium/helium/PE cost inflation; ex-anchor order intake decelerated to ~INR 3,000 cr.
- _Q2 FY27 → check: (a) attach rate actually above 20%, (b) EBITDA margin progress toward 23%, (c) whether the US $100 mn capex phasing and commissioning timeline is finally disclosed as promised, (d) gross-margin recovery as germanium sourcing "improves quarter-on-quarter", (e) order intake ex-anchor — recovery or continued capacity rationing, (f) execution against the INR 2,228 cr Q2 executable book, (g) DC+Enterprise mix tracking to 50%._

outlook.body:
- **EBITDA margin guidance RAISED to 23%** (from the previous "20% by end of FY27", which was delivered in Q1). The stated drivers: improving capacity utilisation, product/customer mix, and a healthier cable+connectivity ratio.
- **Data Center + Enterprise to reach 50% of revenue in the current fiscal** — **raised from the 30% guided on the previous earnings call.**
- **Connectivity attach rate: above 20% from next quarter (Q2 FY27), and 25% by end of this financial year (Q4 FY27)** — currently 16%.
- **Capex: ~INR 500 cr per year for the next 3 years, ~INR 1,500 cr cumulative**, for equipment upgrades across glass/fibre/cable/connectivity plus site de-bottlenecking.
- **US plant: $100 mn investment over a 5-year period** (announced May 2026), primarily a connectivity facility for telecom and DC segments; capex phasing and commissioning timeline **not yet disclosed — "we'll probably update you by next quarter."**
- **Net-debt-free to be maintained through FY27** via QIP proceeds, internal accruals and a working-capital reduction programme (renegotiating customer payment terms).
- **Q2 FY27 executable order book: INR 2,228 cr** — management stressed twice this is *not* revenue guidance (last quarter's INR 1,500 cr executable book preceded a much larger actual execution).
- **Explicitly NOT guided:** full-year revenue, capacity utilisation numbers, realisation, telecom-vs-DC margin split, and the optical-connectivity/cable revenue-EBITDA split.
- **Long-term ambition restated: top 3 in the world** in optical connectivity.

outlook.body:
- **Open order book INR 18,618 cr, up 2.4x QoQ.** Q2 FY27 executable INR 2,228 cr; INR 16,390 cr scheduled for Q3 FY27 onwards.
- **Anchor: a landmark multi-year $1.1 bn deal with a global hyperscaler** to supply optical connectivity for next-gen AI data centres **through FY29**.
- **Multiple separate $100 mn hyperscaler orders** for high-fibre-count IBR cable solutions.
- A **strategic long-haul order with a major connectivity infrastructure provider**.
- Excluding the $1.1 bn anchor, quarterly intake was still ~INR 3,000 cr — down from INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter, which the CFO attributed to capacity-driven selectivity rather than demand: "now we are in a situation wherein we have to pick and choose the orders basis the capacity availability."
- Order book described as **well diversified** across customer segments, product categories and regions.
- Four parallel demand centres named: legacy telecom (growing in pockets, notably the US); hyperscaler/neocloud data centres; neutral-fibre/telco long-haul serving DCs; and rural programmes — **BEAD in the US (5-7 year build-out)** and **BharatNet in India (3-4 year build-out at least)**.

outlook.body:
- **Neuralis** (AI-era DC portfolio) addressing AI white-space connectivity and high-speed DCI. **US Conec certification achieved for MMC pre-terminated solutions**, delivering 3x cable density vs traditional layouts — makes STL one of the few global players with certified MMC trunks, array cords and assemblies for hyperscalers scaling to 800G and beyond.
- **Next-gen fibre:** G.654.E fully commercialised with 30% lower signal loss; **Hollow-Core Fibre cutting latency by up to 47%**; multi-core fibre expanding capacity 4-7x in the same footprint, with real-world deployments in India and the UK alongside C-DOT, IIT Madras and Colt.
- **CONCAT** — spliceless plug-and-play MPO-to-LC FTTH architecture that **cuts labour cost by up to 71%** by moving fibre preparation into the factory; field-validated with a top-tier US operator, Lightwave Innovation Award winner. Strategically it is the attach-rate lever.
- **785+ patents** with 9 new filings in the quarter.
- **Not pursuing:** optical transceivers ("not something that we're looking at currently") and semiconductors — though management noted its glass capability could theoretically serve semiconductor requirements, "not immediately a priority."

outlook.body: STL is deepening its US presence through its Lugoff manufacturing facility, positioning itself to capitalise on reshoring tailwinds as a primary partner for regional broadband and data-centre expansion. In FY26 the company moved next-generation Multi-Core and Hollow-Core fibre technologies out of the laboratory into active customer pilots and secured US Plenum qualifications to unlock high-density enterprise and data-centre environments. It launched Neuralis, a purpose-built connectivity suite for AI data centres, introduced India's first Hollow Core Fibre (HCF) cable, and in the UK rolled out a 4-core Multi-Core Fibre Unitube cable that expanded data capacity per strand. In the US, the company expanded its IBR portfolio to higher fibre counts to enable faster network scaling. STL states it is growing capability through R&D centres, academic partnerships and hiring focused on fiberising AI clusters at scale.

outlook.body:
- Revenue from operations increased 19% from Rs 3,996 crores in FY25 to Rs 4,745 crores in FY26, primarily due to increased demand from Optical Networking Business (ONB) customers in the United States and European regions
- ONB business revenue grew 20% from FY25 to Rs 4,486 crore due to increased sales levels among customers in the United States and European regions
- In its third year of operation, the Digital and technology solutions business (Digital) reported revenue of Rs 284 crore in FY26, on the back of a strong order book
- AI-driven fibre demand: hyperscaler AI data-centre buildouts are transitioning server-rack infrastructure from copper to fibre, with denser GPU clusters requiring exponentially higher fibre counts per rack
- North American FTTH market shows signs of strong recovery as carriers resume expanding optical networks, supported by Tier-1 telco capex and government programmes, with a multi-year FTTH-led fibre cycle continuing
- APAC (ex-China) demand is accelerating on infrastructure mandates, with new-build rollouts in India, Saudi Arabia and African markets, while mature markets like South Korea and Japan shift capital to high-value upgrades
- European FTTH sector is transitioning from intensive infrastructure deployment toward network monetisation and regional consolidation, with a divergence between mature markets (deceleration) and active rollouts in the UK and Germany
- 5G/6G network densification and edge/enterprise AI adoption (CIOs increasingly allocating budget to AI-related networking) are structural long-term demand drivers for optical fibre in backhaul and fronthaul networks
- Emerging secular demand from defence/drone applications is a further driver of fibre demand and pricing
- The industry continues to show signs of recovery with long-term growth supporting continued growth and a path to global leadership
- A sharply expanding order book, alongside revenue growth and improving margins, strengthened the company in FY26
- The Digital and technology solutions business reported FY26 revenue on the back of a strong order book

deepdive.thesis: The quarter STL's data-centre thesis converted into numbers: revenue INR 1,910 cr (+87% YoY), EBITDA INR 397 cr (+184%), PAT INR 197 cr — a record on all three — with **Q1 order intake of INR 13,100 cr, 1.7x the entire FY26 order book**, anchored by a multi-year **$1.1 bn hyperscaler deal running through FY29**. The binding constraint has flipped from demand to capacity and raw materials (germanium, helium) — STL is now "pick and choose" on orders.

one-line thesis: The quarter STL's data-centre thesis converted into numbers: revenue INR 1,910 cr (+87% YoY), EBITDA INR 397 cr (+184%), PAT INR 197 cr — a record on all three — with **Q1 order intake of INR 13,100 cr, 1.7x the entire FY26 order book**, anchored by a multi-year **$1.1 bn hyperscaler deal running through FY29**. Management hit its 20%-by-end-FY27 EBITDA margin target in Q1 and immediately **raised the target to 23%**, while the DC+Enterprise mix guidance went from 30% to 50% of FY27 revenue. The binding constraint has flipped from demand to capacity and raw materials (germanium, helium) — STL is now "pick and choose" on orders.
financial scorecard (track qoq/yoy):
| Metric | Q1FY27 | YoY | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | **INR 1,910 cr** | **+87%** | Highest ever |
| EBITDA / margin | **INR 397 cr / 20.8%** | +184% | Delivered the FY27-exit 20% target in Q1 |
| PAT | **INR 197 cr / 10.3% margin** | 3.5x full-year FY26 PAT | Highest-ever PAT margin |
| Gross margin | broadly flat sequentially | — | Input-cost (germanium/helium/polyethylene) pressure offset the DC mix benefit |
| Order intake (quarter) | **INR 13,100 cr** | 1.7x total FY26 wins of INR 7,687 cr | Anchored by the $1.1 bn hyperscaler deal |
| Open order book | **INR 18,618 cr** | **+2.4x QoQ** | INR 2,228 cr executable in Q2 FY27; INR 16,390 cr in Q3 FY27 and beyond |
| Cash / net debt | **Net cash INR 483 cr — net-debt-free** | — | CRISIL outlook revised to Stable; ICRA upgraded to AA Stable |
| DC segment share | 21% of revenue | from 1% in FY26 | DC + Enterprise guided to 50% for FY27 |
| Geography mix | North America 54% · Europe 25% · RoW 22% | NA up from 39% in FY26 | — |
| Market share / attach rate | 9% global ex-China OFC share; connectivity attach rate 16% | attach up from 15% | On a much larger OFC revenue base |
> **Adjustments / one-offs:** a **INR 1,500 cr QIP** was completed in the quarter (subscribed >2.5x; Nomura, HSBC, Motilal Oswal, Bank of India among investors), taking institutional holding to a historic-high 33%; **75% of proceeds go to debt reduction**, the balance to general corporate purposes — this is what produced the net-debt-free status. A **European patent dispute with Fujikura was conclusively resolved in STL's favour**, closing the UK litigation over the Celesta cable family and removing legal overhang from the DC and telecom business.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **EBITDA margin guidance RAISED to 23%** (from the previous "20% by end of FY27", which was delivered in Q1). The stated drivers: improving capacity utilisation, product/customer mix, and a healthier cable+connectivity ratio.
- **Data Center + Enterprise to reach 50% of revenue in the current fiscal** — **raised from the 30% guided on the previous earnings call.**
- **Connectivity attach rate: above 20% from next quarter (Q2 FY27), and 25% by end of this financial year (Q4 FY27)** — currently 16%.
- **Capex: ~INR 500 cr per year for the next 3 years, ~INR 1,500 cr cumulative**, for equipment upgrades across glass/fibre/cable/connectivity plus site de-bottlenecking.
- **US plant: $100 mn investment over a 5-year period** (announced May 2026), primarily a connectivity facility for telecom and DC segments; capex phasing and commissioning timeline **not yet disclosed — "we'll probably update you by next quarter."**
- **Net-debt-free to be maintained through FY27** via QIP proceeds, internal accruals and a working-capital reduction programme (renegotiating customer payment terms).
- **Q2 FY27 executable order book: INR 2,228 cr** — management stressed twice this is *not* revenue guidance (last quarter's INR 1,500 cr executable book preceded a much larger actual execution).
- **Explicitly NOT guided:** full-year revenue, capacity utilisation numbers, realisation, telecom-vs-DC margin split, and the optical-connectivity/cable revenue-EBITDA split.
- **Long-term ambition restated: top 3 in the world** in optical connectivity.
order book & pipeline:
- **Open order book INR 18,618 cr, up 2.4x QoQ.** Q2 FY27 executable INR 2,228 cr; INR 16,390 cr scheduled for Q3 FY27 onwards.
- **Anchor: a landmark multi-year $1.1 bn deal with a global hyperscaler** to supply optical connectivity for next-gen AI data centres **through FY29**.
- **Multiple separate $100 mn hyperscaler orders** for high-fibre-count IBR cable solutions.
- A **strategic long-haul order with a major connectivity infrastructure provider**.
- Excluding the $1.1 bn anchor, quarterly intake was still ~INR 3,000 cr — down from INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter, which the CFO attributed to capacity-driven selectivity rather than demand: "now we are in a situation wherein we have to pick and choose the orders basis the capacity availability."
- Order book described as **well diversified** across customer segments, product categories and regions.
- Four parallel demand centres named: legacy telecom (growing in pockets, notably the US); hyperscaler/neocloud data centres; neutral-fibre/telco long-haul serving DCs; and rural programmes — **BEAD in the US (5-7 year build-out)** and **BharatNet in India (3-4 year build-out at least)**.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Data Center: 21% of Q1 revenue, up from 1% in FY26** — the single largest mix shift in the business.
- **Telecom & Citizen Networks** remains the core pillar; management is deliberate about keeping it as the counterweight to DC cyclicality.
- **Geography:** North America expanded to 54% of revenue (from 39% in FY26), Europe 25%, RoW 22%. CRU's North America CAGR forecast to 2030 was upgraded from 15% to **18.6%**.
- **US onshore:** South Carolina facility supports the Neuralis MMC pre-terminated launch; the new $100 mn investment is a connectivity (not fibre-capacity) facility — "it doesn't really translate into a capacity per se."
- Businesses deliberately exited: active components, multiple other lines, and the system-integration business (demerged) — "a very conscious choice to be very, very focused on the optical fiber cable connectivity side."
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Neuralis** (AI-era DC portfolio) addressing AI white-space connectivity and high-speed DCI. **US Conec certification achieved for MMC pre-terminated solutions**, delivering 3x cable density vs traditional layouts — makes STL one of the few global players with certified MMC trunks, array cords and assemblies for hyperscalers scaling to 800G and beyond.
- **Next-gen fibre:** G.654.E fully commercialised with 30% lower signal loss; **Hollow-Core Fibre cutting latency by up to 47%**; multi-core fibre expanding capacity 4-7x in the same footprint, with real-world deployments in India and the UK alongside C-DOT, IIT Madras and Colt.
- **CONCAT** — spliceless plug-and-play MPO-to-LC FTTH architecture that **cuts labour cost by up to 71%** by moving fibre preparation into the factory; field-validated with a top-tier US operator, Lightwave Innovation Award winner. Strategically it is the attach-rate lever.
- **785+ patents** with 9 new filings in the quarter.
- **Not pursuing:** optical transceivers ("not something that we're looking at currently") and semiconductors — though management noted its glass capability could theoretically serve semiconductor requirements, "not immediately a priority."
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Glass-to-gigabit vertical integration** — silicon tetrachloride formation, CVD, high-precision sintering to ultra-pure preforms, then fibre draw, high-density cable design and connectivity. "We are amongst the very few companies in the world to have mastered the journey from glass to gigabit," and it is the stated source of quality, cost and innovation edge.
- **Certification as a barrier:** US Conec MMC certification puts STL among "the few global players" able to serve hyperscalers at 800G+ density.
- **Litigation risk eliminated:** definitive victory over Fujikura in the European patent dispute closes the UK Celesta litigation — "removes all legal uncertainty around these products."
- **Rating upgrades** (ICRA to AA Stable, CRISIL outlook to Stable) plus net-debt-free status — a balance-sheet moat in a capital-intensive industry where lead times are tightening.
- Global ex-China OFC share at 9%, gaining "despite broader environmental challenges."
- World's first optical fibre manufacturer certified for zero liquid discharge and zero waste to landfill.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin of ~20.8% was achieved a full year ahead of the previous guide, but **gross margin was broadly flat sequentially despite a richer DC mix** — the CFO attributed this squarely to input costs: "the prices of the key raw material getting increased to significant multiples" in the war situation. The three named raw-material exposures are **germanium** (glass process — dual response of diversifying sources *and* developing technology to reduce consumption per unit), **helium** (fibre manufacturing — recycling technology already in place, watching Middle East developments closely), and **polyethylene** (oil-linked, and "up to a certain level… we are able to pass that on to our customers"). The path to 23% is therefore three levers management named explicitly: higher factory utilisation, better product/customer mix, and the attach-rate climb from 16% → 20%+ → 25%. DC solutions carry structurally higher margins than telecom, which management confirmed without quantifying.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **~INR 500 cr/yr for 3 years (INR 1,500 cr total)** on equipment upgrades and de-bottlenecking across glass, fibre, cable and connectivity — explicitly *not* a greenfield capacity programme.
- **$100 mn US investment over 5 years** — announced May 2026, but with **no capex phasing and no commissioning timeline disclosed**; management committed to update "by next quarter." This is the clearest slippage-watch item.
- Capacity utilisation is deliberately undisclosed but "improving quarter-on-quarter." De-bottlenecking and upgrades are running in parallel with active customer conversations for further orders, so incremental capacity and incremental orders are being matched rather than pre-built.
capital allocation: The INR 1,500 cr QIP is the defining capital event: **75% to debt reduction**, balance to general corporate purposes, taking the company to net cash INR 483 cr. Institutional holding reached a historic-high 33%. Beyond deleveraging, capital goes to a modest INR 500 cr/yr equipment programme and the $100 mn US connectivity facility over five years — i.e. capital-light growth funded by utilisation and de-bottlenecking rather than greenfield. Working capital is a stated focus, "engaging into dialogues with the customers on reducing the payment terms." Notably absent: any large capacity capex despite an order book that is 2.4x larger and a demand environment where lead times are tightening.
risks & watch-items:
- **Raw-material availability is the binding operational risk.** Germanium sourcing is "work in progress over the next few quarters"; helium is being watched against Middle East developments. Management is taking orders "keeping in mind the availability of our raw materials" — i.e. the order book is already being rationed against input risk.
- **Capacity is the second constraint** — orders are being picked and chosen; ex-anchor intake fell from INR 7,000-8,000 cr to ~INR 3,000 cr. If de-bottlenecking underdelivers, the order book converts more slowly.
- **Order-book concentration:** the $1.1 bn hyperscaler deal is a very large share of the INR 18,618 cr book, and INR 16,390 cr of it executes in Q3 FY27 *and beyond* — the near-term executable slice is only INR 2,228 cr.
- **Hyperscaler capex cyclicality**, plus the analyst-raised question of Chinese token-cost deflation compressing the AI capex environment. Management's answer was macro-thesis-based (cloud revenues accelerating, demand outstripping supply) but conceded "the price points will have to become more efficient" and "there has to be something that has to give at some level."
- **No revenue guidance at all** — management repeated they don't guide and cannot say how much they will grow from here.
- Europe DC investment "progress and speed on the ground is still slow"; framed as "a dark horse" that scales in a year or two — i.e. 25% of revenue sits in a region management describes as behind.
management quality / tone: Confident and specific where it counts — raised two guidance items (margin 20%→23%, DC+Enterprise mix 30%→50%) rather than merely reaffirming, and pre-emptively corrected an analyst who was reading the executable order book as revenue guidance. Disclosure discipline is consistent and pre-declared: capacity utilisation, realisation, germanium contracting terms and segment margin splits are all refused "for competitive reasons," which is defensible but does limit verification. The most credible moment was the CFO answering the gross-margin question honestly against interest — acknowledging raw-material pressure rather than attributing flat gross margin to mix timing. Ankit Agarwal's answer on the AI/telecom balance was strategically thoughtful rather than promotional, explicitly wanting the telecom and rural (BharatNet/BEAD) books as ballast against DC cyclicality.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **Ex the anchor deal, order intake actually decelerated** — INR ~3,000 cr this quarter vs INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter. The CFO's framing (capacity-driven selectivity, not demand weakness) is plausible given the "pick and choose" comment, but it is the number to watch if utilisation improves and intake does *not* recover.
- **Margin was raised while gross margin was flat.** The entire 20%→23% bridge sits below the gross line: utilisation, mix, attach rate. That makes the attach-rate milestones (>20% in Q2, 25% by Q4) the most load-bearing checkable commitments on the call.
- **STL is deliberately capital-light into a demand boom** — INR 500 cr/yr of upgrades against an INR 18,618 cr book. It is choosing de-bottlenecking over greenfield, which protects returns but caps how much of the AI cycle it can capture.
- The **$100 mn US facility is a connectivity plant, not fibre capacity** — it does not add cable/fibre tonnage; its purpose is onshore turnaround speed and product customisation for US DC customers.
- Management explicitly closed the door on transceivers and semiconductors, the two adjacencies the market most often extrapolates for an AI-DC optical play.

one_liner.body: STL is a leading global optical company delivering advanced optical connectivity capabilities to telecom operators, hyperscale cloud companies, citizen networks and large enterprises.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: STL designs, manufactures and deploys advanced optical connectivity solutions (optical fibre, cable and data-centre interconnect products) for telecom operators, hyperscale cloud companies, citizen/government broadband networks and large enterprises. Through STL Neox it also offers a Unified Communications platform (UCaaS, CCaaS, CPaaS) built on IP technology, and through STL Digital it provides digital/IT services.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body:
- **Data Center: 21% of Q1 revenue, up from 1% in FY26** — the single largest mix shift in the business.
- **Telecom & Citizen Networks** remains the core pillar; management is deliberate about keeping it as the counterweight to DC cyclicality.
- **Geography:** North America expanded to 54% of revenue (from 39% in FY26), Europe 25%, RoW 22%. CRU's North America CAGR forecast to 2030 was upgraded from 15% to **18.6%**.
- **US onshore:** South Carolina facility supports the Neuralis MMC pre-terminated launch; the new $100 mn investment is a connectivity (not fibre-capacity) facility — "it doesn't really translate into a capacity per se."
- Businesses deliberately exited: active components, multiple other lines, and the system-integration business (demerged) — "a very conscious choice to be very, very focused on the optical fiber cable connectivity side."

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body:
- **Open order book INR 18,618 cr, up 2.4x QoQ.** Q2 FY27 executable INR 2,228 cr; INR 16,390 cr scheduled for Q3 FY27 onwards.
- **Anchor: a landmark multi-year $1.1 bn deal with a global hyperscaler** to supply optical connectivity for next-gen AI data centres **through FY29**.
- **Multiple separate $100 mn hyperscaler orders** for high-fibre-count IBR cable solutions.
- A **strategic long-haul order with a major connectivity infrastructure provider**.
- Excluding the $1.1 bn anchor, quarterly intake was still ~INR 3,000 cr — down from INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter, which the CFO attributed to capacity-driven selectivity rather than demand: "now we are in a situation wherein we have to pick and choose the orders basis the capacity availability."
- Order book described as **well diversified** across customer segments, product categories and regions.
- Four parallel demand centres named: legacy telecom (growing in pockets, notably the US); hyperscaler/neocloud data centres; neutral-fibre/telco long-haul serving DCs; and rural programmes — **BEAD in the US (5-7 year build-out)** and **BharatNet in India (3-4 year build-out at least)**.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
- **EBITDA margin guidance RAISED to 23%** (from the previous "20% by end of FY27", which was delivered in Q1). The stated drivers: improving capacity utilisation, product/customer mix, and a healthier cable+connectivity ratio.
- **Data Center + Enterprise to reach 50% of revenue in the current fiscal** — **raised from the 30% guided on the previous earnings call.**
- **Connectivity attach rate: above 20% from next quarter (Q2 FY27), and 25% by end of this financial year (Q4 FY27)** — currently 16%.
- **Capex: ~INR 500 cr per year for the next 3 years, ~INR 1,500 cr cumulative**, for equipment upgrades across glass/fibre/cable/connectivity plus site de-bottlenecking.
- **US plant: $100 mn investment over a 5-year period** (announced May 2026), primarily a connectivity facility for telecom and DC segments; capex phasing and commissioning timeline **not yet disclosed — "we'll probably update you by next quarter."**
- **Net-debt-free to be maintained through FY27** via QIP proceeds, internal accruals and a working-capital reduction programme (renegotiating customer payment terms).
- **Q2 FY27 executable order book: INR 2,228 cr** — management stressed twice this is *not* revenue guidance (last quarter's INR 1,500 cr executable book preceded a much larger actual execution).
- **Explicitly NOT guided:** full-year revenue, capacity utilisation numbers, realisation, telecom-vs-DC margin split, and the optical-connectivity/cable revenue-EBITDA split.
- **Long-term ambition restated: top 3 in the world** in optical connectivity.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **Neuralis** (AI-era DC portfolio) addressing AI white-space connectivity and high-speed DCI. **US Conec certification achieved for MMC pre-terminated solutions**, delivering 3x cable density vs traditional layouts — makes STL one of the few global players with certified MMC trunks, array cords and assemblies for hyperscalers scaling to 800G and beyond.
- **Next-gen fibre:** G.654.E fully commercialised with 30% lower signal loss; **Hollow-Core Fibre cutting latency by up to 47%**; multi-core fibre expanding capacity 4-7x in the same footprint, with real-world deployments in India and the UK alongside C-DOT, IIT Madras and Colt.
- **CONCAT** — spliceless plug-and-play MPO-to-LC FTTH architecture that **cuts labour cost by up to 71%** by moving fibre preparation into the factory; field-validated with a top-tier US operator, Lightwave Innovation Award winner. Strategically it is the attach-rate lever.
- **785+ patents** with 9 new filings in the quarter.
- **Not pursuing:** optical transceivers ("not something that we're looking at currently") and semiconductors — though management noted its glass capability could theoretically serve semiconductor requirements, "not immediately a priority."

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Revenue from operations increased 19% from Rs 3,996 crores in FY25 to Rs 4,745 crores in FY26, primarily due to increased demand from Optical Networking Business (ONB) customers in the United States and European regions
- ONB business revenue grew 20% from FY25 to Rs 4,486 crore due to increased sales levels among customers in the United States and European regions
- In its third year of operation, the Digital and technology solutions business (Digital) reported revenue of Rs 284 crore in FY26, on the back of a strong order book
- AI-driven fibre demand: hyperscaler AI data-centre buildouts are transitioning server-rack infrastructure from copper to fibre, with denser GPU clusters requiring exponentially higher fibre counts per rack
- North American FTTH market shows signs of strong recovery as carriers resume expanding optical networks, supported by Tier-1 telco capex and government programmes, with a multi-year FTTH-led fibre cycle continuing
- APAC (ex-China) demand is accelerating on infrastructure mandates, with new-build rollouts in India, Saudi Arabia and African markets, while mature markets like South Korea and Japan shift capital to high-value upgrades
- European FTTH sector is transitioning from intensive infrastructure deployment toward network monetisation and regional consolidation, with a divergence between mature markets (deceleration) and active rollouts in the UK and Germany
- 5G/6G network densification and edge/enterprise AI adoption (CIOs increasingly allocating budget to AI-related networking) are structural long-term demand drivers for optical fibre in backhaul and fronthaul networks
- Emerging secular demand from defence/drone applications is a further driver of fibre demand and pricing
- The industry continues to show signs of recovery with long-term growth supporting continued growth and a path to global leadership
- A sharply expanding order book, alongside revenue growth and improving margins, strengthened the company in FY26
- The Digital and technology solutions business reported FY26 revenue on the back of a strong order book

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA margin of ~20.8% was achieved a full year ahead of the previous guide, but **gross margin was broadly flat sequentially despite a richer DC mix** — the CFO attributed this squarely to input costs: "the prices of the key raw material getting increased to significant multiples" in the war situation. The three named raw-material exposures are **germanium** (glass process — dual response of diversifying sources *and* developing technology to reduce consumption per unit), **helium** (fibre manufacturing — recycling technology already in place, watching Middle East developments closely), and **polyethylene** (oil-linked, and "up to a certain level… we are able to pass that on to our customers"). The path to 23% is therefore three levers management named explicitly: higher factory utilisation, better product/customer mix, and the attach-rate climb from 16% → 20%+ → 25%. DC solutions carry structurally higher margins than telecom, which management confirmed without quantifying.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: The INR 1,500 cr QIP is the defining capital event: **75% to debt reduction**, balance to general corporate purposes, taking the company to net cash INR 483 cr. Institutional holding reached a historic-high 33%. Beyond deleveraging, capital goes to a modest INR 500 cr/yr equipment programme and the $100 mn US connectivity facility over five years — i.e. capital-light growth funded by utilisation and de-bottlenecking rather than greenfield. Working capital is a stated focus, "engaging into dialogues with the customers on reducing the payment terms." Notably absent: any large capacity capex despite an order book that is 2.4x larger and a demand environment where lead times are tightening.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: STL is deepening its US presence through its Lugoff manufacturing facility, positioning itself to capitalise on reshoring tailwinds as a primary partner for regional broadband and data-centre expansion. In FY26 the company moved next-generation Multi-Core and Hollow-Core fibre technologies out of the laboratory into active customer pilots and secured US Plenum qualifications to unlock high-density enterprise and data-centre environments. It launched Neuralis, a purpose-built connectivity suite for AI data centres, introduced India's first Hollow Core Fibre (HCF) cable, and in the UK rolled out a 4-core Multi-Core Fibre Unitube cable that expanded data capacity per strand. In the US, the company expanded its IBR portfolio to higher fibre counts to enable faster network scaling. STL states it is growing capability through R&D centres, academic partnerships and hiring focused on fiberising AI clusters at scale.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and specific where it counts — raised two guidance items (margin 20%→23%, DC+Enterprise mix 30%→50%) rather than merely reaffirming, and pre-emptively corrected an analyst who was reading the executable order book as revenue guidance. Disclosure discipline is consistent and pre-declared: capacity utilisation, realisation, germanium contracting terms and segment margin splits are all refused "for competitive reasons," which is defensible but does limit verification. The most credible moment was the CFO answering the gross-margin question honestly against interest — acknowledging raw-material pressure rather than attributing flat gross margin to mix timing. Ankit Agarwal's answer on the AI/telecom balance was strategically thoughtful rather than promotional, explicitly wanting the telecom and rural (BharatNet/BEAD) books as ballast against DC cyclicality.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrates glass science with precision manufacturing to co-create advanced high-density, low-latency optical solutions
- Claims first-mover next-generation fibre products - India's first Hollow Core Fibre cable and a 4-core Multi-Core Fibre Unitube cable launched in the UK
- CONCAT pre-connectorised, plug-and-play solution is designed to reduce on-site labour and cut installation timelines versus conventional deployment
- Global manufacturing and commercial footprint spanning the US, Europe, India and China
- New FY26 customer partnerships with operators including Colt, Netomnia, Mynet, SLICFiber and Swoop

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Raw-material availability is the binding operational risk.** Germanium sourcing is "work in progress over the next few quarters"; helium is being watched against Middle East developments. Management is taking orders "keeping in mind the availability of our raw materials" — i.e. the order book is already being rationed against input risk.
- **Capacity is the second constraint** — orders are being picked and chosen; ex-anchor intake fell from INR 7,000-8,000 cr to ~INR 3,000 cr. If de-bottlenecking underdelivers, the order book converts more slowly.
- **Order-book concentration:** the $1.1 bn hyperscaler deal is a very large share of the INR 18,618 cr book, and INR 16,390 cr of it executes in Q3 FY27 *and beyond* — the near-term executable slice is only INR 2,228 cr.
- **Hyperscaler capex cyclicality**, plus the analyst-raised question of Chinese token-cost deflation compressing the AI capex environment. Management's answer was macro-thesis-based (cloud revenues accelerating, demand outstripping supply) but conceded "the price points will have to become more efficient" and "there has to be something that has to give at some level."
- **No revenue guidance at all** — management repeated they don't guide and cannot say how much they will grow from here.
- Europe DC investment "progress and speed on the ground is still slow"; framed as "a dark horse" that scales in a year or two — i.e. 25% of revenue sits in a region management describes as behind.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **Ex the anchor deal, order intake actually decelerated** — INR ~3,000 cr this quarter vs INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter. The CFO's framing (capacity-driven selectivity, not demand weakness) is plausible given the "pick and choose" comment, but it is the number to watch if utilisation improves and intake does *not* recover.
- **Margin was raised while gross margin was flat.** The entire 20%→23% bridge sits below the gross line: utilisation, mix, attach rate. That makes the attach-rate milestones (>20% in Q2, 25% by Q4) the most load-bearing checkable commitments on the call.
- **STL is deliberately capital-light into a demand boom** — INR 500 cr/yr of upgrades against an INR 18,618 cr book. It is choosing de-bottlenecking over greenfield, which protects returns but caps how much of the AI cycle it can capture.
- The **$100 mn US facility is a connectivity plant, not fibre capacity** — it does not add cable/fibre tonnage; its purpose is onshore turnaround speed and product customisation for US DC customers.
- Management explicitly closed the door on transceivers and semiconductors, the two adjacencies the market most often extrapolates for an AI-DC optical play.

qoq_log.title: QoQ change log (fill each quarter)
qoq_log.body:
- **Q4 FY26 (prior):** order book INR 7.3k cr; **targeting 20% EBITDA margin by end of FY27**; FY26 inflows doubled to INR 7,687 cr; ~INR 500 cr capex planned for technology upgrades and high-value DC portfolio; DC + Enterprise guided at 30% of revenue.
- **Q1 FY27 (this):** *Guidance beaten and raised:* the 20% EBITDA margin target for end-FY27 was **hit in Q1** and the target **raised to 23%**; DC+Enterprise mix guidance **raised from 30% to 50%** of FY27 revenue. *Delivered:* INR 500 cr/yr capex confirmed and extended to a 3-year INR 1,500 cr programme; DC revenue share went 1% (FY26) → 21%. *Step-change:* Q1 order intake of INR 13,100 cr = 1.7x all of FY26; open order book INR 18,618 cr (+2.4x QoQ) vs INR 7.3k cr last quarter; net-debt-free after a INR 1,500 cr QIP (75% to debt reduction); ICRA upgrade to AA Stable. *New commitments:* attach rate >20% from Q2 FY27 and 25% by Q4 FY27; $100 mn US connectivity plant over 5 years (phasing TBD); $1.1 bn hyperscaler contract running to FY29. *Watch:* gross margin flat despite mix, on germanium/helium/PE cost inflation; ex-anchor order intake decelerated to ~INR 3,000 cr.
- _Q2 FY27 → check: (a) attach rate actually above 20%, (b) EBITDA margin progress toward 23%, (c) whether the US $100 mn capex phasing and commissioning timeline is finally disclosed as promised, (d) gross-margin recovery as germanium sourcing "improves quarter-on-quarter", (e) order intake ex-anchor — recovery or continued capacity rationing, (f) execution against the INR 2,228 cr Q2 executable book, (g) DC+Enterprise mix tracking to 50%._

- **Not pursuing:** optical transceivers ("not something that we're looking at currently") and semiconductors — though management noted its glass capability could theoretically serve semiconductor requirements, "not immediately a priority."
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Glass-to-gigabit vertical integration** — silicon tetrachloride formation, CVD, high-precision sintering to ultra-pure preforms, then fibre draw, high-density cable design and connectivity. "We are amongst the very few companies in the world to have mastered the journey from glass to gigabit," and it is the stated source of quality, cost and innovation edge.
- **Certification as a barrier:** US Conec MMC certification puts STL among "the few global players" able to serve hyperscalers at 800G+ density.
- **Litigation risk eliminated:** definitive victory over Fujikura in the European patent dispute closes the UK Celesta litigation — "removes all legal uncertainty around these products."
- **Rating upgrades** (ICRA to AA Stable, CRISIL outlook to Stable) plus net-debt-free status — a balance-sheet moat in a capital-intensive industry where lead times are tightening.
- Global ex-China OFC share at 9%, gaining "despite broader environmental challenges."
- World's first optical fibre manufacturer certified for zero liquid discharge and zero waste to landfill.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin of ~20.8% was achieved a full year ahead of the previous guide, but **gross margin was broadly flat sequentially despite a richer DC mix** — the CFO attributed this squarely to input costs: "the prices of the key raw material getting increased to significant multiples" in the war situation. The three named raw-material exposures are **germanium** (glass process — dual response of diversifying sources *and* developing technology to reduce consumption per unit), **helium** (fibre manufacturing — recycling technology already in place, watching Middle East developments closely), and **polyethylene** (oil-linked, and "up to a certain level… we are able to pass that on to our customers"). The path to 23% is therefore three levers management named explicitly: higher factory utilisation, better product/customer mix, and the attach-rate climb from 16% → 20%+ → 25%. DC solutions carry structurally higher margins than telecom, which management confirmed without quantifying.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **~INR 500 cr/yr for 3 years (INR 1,500 cr total)** on equipment upgrades and de-bottlenecking across glass, fibre, cable and connectivity — explicitly *not* a greenfield capacity programme.
- **$100 mn US investment over 5 years** — announced May 2026, but with **no capex phasing and no commissioning timeline disclosed**; management committed to update "by next quarter." This is the clearest slippage-watch item.
- Capacity utilisation is deliberately undisclosed but "improving quarter-on-quarter." De-bottlenecking and upgrades are running in parallel with active customer conversations for further orders, so incremental capacity and incremental orders are being matched rather than pre-built.
capital allocation: The INR 1,500 cr QIP is the defining capital event: **75% to debt reduction**, balance to general corporate purposes, taking the company to net cash INR 483 cr. Institutional holding reached a historic-high 33%. Beyond deleveraging, capital goes to a modest INR 500 cr/yr equipment programme and the $100 mn US connectivity facility over five years — i.e. capital-light growth funded by utilisation and de-bottlenecking rather than greenfield. Working capital is a stated focus, "engaging into dialogues with the customers on reducing the payment terms." Notably absent: any large capacity capex despite an order book that is 2.4x larger and a demand environment where lead times are tightening.
risks & watch-items:
- **Raw-material availability is the binding operational risk.** Germanium sourcing is "work in progress over the next few quarters"; helium is being watched against Middle East developments. Management is taking orders "keeping in mind the availability of our raw materials" — i.e. the order book is already being rationed against input risk.
- **Capacity is the second constraint** — orders are being picked and chosen; ex-anchor intake fell from INR 7,000-8,000 cr to ~INR 3,000 cr. If de-bottlenecking underdelivers, the order book converts more slowly.
- **Order-book concentration:** the $1.1 bn hyperscaler deal is a very large share of the INR 18,618 cr book, and INR 16,390 cr of it executes in Q3 FY27 *and beyond* — the near-term executable slice is only INR 2,228 cr.
- **Hyperscaler capex cyclicality**, plus the analyst-raised question of Chinese token-cost deflation compressing the AI capex environment. Management's answer was macro-thesis-based (cloud revenues accelerating, demand outstripping supply) but conceded "the price points will have to become more efficient" and "there has to be something that has to give at some level."
- **No revenue guidance at all** — management repeated they don't guide and cannot say how much they will grow from here.
- Europe DC investment "progress and speed on the ground is still slow"; framed as "a dark horse" that scales in a year or two — i.e. 25% of revenue sits in a region management describes as behind.
management quality / tone: Confident and specific where it counts — raised two guidance items (margin 20%→23%, DC+Enterprise mix 30%→50%) rather than merely reaffirming, and pre-emptively corrected an analyst who was reading the executable order book as revenue guidance. Disclosure discipline is consistent and pre-declared: capacity utilisation, realisation, germanium contracting terms and segment margin splits are all refused "for competitive reasons," which is defensible but does limit verification. The most credible moment was the CFO answering the gross-margin question honestly against interest — acknowledging raw-material pressure rather than attributing flat gross margin to mix timing. Ankit Agarwal's answer on the AI/telecom balance was strategically thoughtful rather than promotional, explicitly wanting the telecom and rural (BharatNet/BEAD) books as ballast against DC cyclicality.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **Ex the anchor deal, order intake actually decelerated** — INR ~3,000 cr this quarter vs INR 7,000-8,000 cr in the prior quarter. The CFO's framing (capacity-driven selectivity, not demand weakness) is plausible given the "pick and choose" comment, but it is the number to watch if utilisation improves and intake does *not* recover.
- **Margin was raised while gross margin was flat.** The entire 20%→23% bridge sits below the gross line: utilisation, mix, attach rate. That makes the attach-rate milestones (>20% in Q2, 25% by Q4) the most load-bearing checkable commitments on the call.
- **STL is deliberately capital-light into a demand boom** — INR 500 cr/yr of upgrades against an INR 18,618 cr book. It is choosing de-bottlenecking over greenfield, which protects returns but caps how much of the AI cycle it can capture.
- The **$100 mn US facility is a connectivity plant, not fibre capacity** — it does not add cable/fibre tonnage; its purpose is onshore turnaround speed and product customisation for US DC customers.
- Management explicitly closed the door on transceivers and semiconductors, the two adjacencies the market most often extrapolates for an AI-DC optical play.
